processing: A green tea finished in three shapes: flat and straight, fine and strip-like, or curled. Each is heated to stop oxidation, then shaped and dried.
harvest_season: Specific dates are not well recorded. As with other Sichuan greens, spring tea is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Depending on style, flat and glossy green, fine and tender green strips, or tight grey-green curls.
appearance_wet: Tender, even shoots that open into whole, bright little clusters.
taste_profile: Flat and strip styles are fresh and brisk with a clean aroma; the curled style is fuller and sweeter. All three have a soft sweet return.

brewing.notes: Plump buds and thick leaf take repeat steeps well. Drop the temperature a little for the most tender flat grades.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring harvest, best within about a year, like other Chinese greens. Since the name covers three shapes and many local product names, ask which style you are buying.
description:
Mabian green tea comes from the Mabian Yi Autonomous County in Leshan, on the southern edge of the Sichuan basin. It is less one tea than a local family: the protected name covers flat, strip and curled styles.

The county is damp and misty, averaging 16.9°C with about 1044 mm of rain a year, on largely purple soils that lean acidic. The tea is locally known for plump buds and thick leaf, which is why it is said to stand up to repeat steeps.

The flat and strip styles are the fresh ones, with a clear aroma and a brisk feel. The curled style has more weight and sweetness, so it suits anyone who finds young greens thin. Brew all of them around 85°C and shorten the steep if bitterness appears.

Look for the style and picking season on the pack. Mabian teas have carried many product names over the years, including Baiyan Yingchun, so a name alone tells you little about the shape or grade.
history:
A local legend ties wild tea here to Zhuge Liang's southern campaign, with soldiers cured of a poisoned spring by tea and herbs. Written tradition is more modest: cultivation is said to have begun in the mid-Ming dynasty, connected with Buddhist monks, as noted in a Qing Jiaqing-era local gazetteer.

In 1930 a trial factory bought raw leaf and sold improved teas under names such as Longhu and Fengmei. Local accounts say the tea was presented to Mao Zedong in 1959, and several products became Sichuan provincial famous teas in the 1980s. It was registered as an agricultural geographical indication on 3 December 2008.
